extracted.intended_audience: authors and programmers learning/using plain TeX for typesetting (TeX users, document authors, format designers)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, conventions, and practical guidance from a plain TeX manual (The TeXbook) covering characters/category codes, fonts/ligatures, accents/special letters, dimension units and syntax, magnification behavior, and box model (hbox/vbox) usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frequent changes to category codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not change TeX category codes often; characters never change their categories once they have become tokens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Category-code changes must be timed carefully because when macro arguments are first scanned they are placed into token lists and their categories are fixed then. The author intentionally uses numeric category codes (not mnemonic names) to discourage casual 
\catcode changes. Only change category codes in unusual circumstances and remember tokens already scanned keep their categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro arguments are tokenized at scan time
rubrics_metrics.description: When arguments to a macro are scanned they are placed into a token list, fixing the category codes of characters at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because categories are fixed when tokenized, later changes to category codes do not affect already-tokenized text. Plan category/code changes with that in mind (e.g., if you temporarily change catcodes to read verbatim text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain TeX uses the roman font by default
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX will use the roman font (\rm or \tenrm) for text unless you specify otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most ordinary symbols, letters A–Z, digits 0–9 and common punctuation are available in \rm. The same input conventions generally apply to \bf, \sl, and \it so you usually don't need different typing for those typefaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligatures are produced automatically in text fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain letter combinations are recognized as ligatures by TeX and are typeset as single glyphs (e.g., ff, fi, fl, ffi, ffl, ``--'' for en/em dashes, ``'''' for quotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware ligatures occur automatically in text fonts; if you want to avoid them (e.g., in typewriter font), switch font or use explicit constructions. Example: in \tt ligatures like ff/fi are not formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregate mathematics from text (use math mode for operators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters such as + and = should be used in math mode ($...$) to get proper mathematical spacing; formulas and text should be segregated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type + and = between $ signs for proper spacing; use the non-mathematical hyphen and slash (- and / outside math) for textual hyphenation and slashes; use - and / inside math for subtraction and division. This preserves correct spacing and semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escape TeX's special characters in text
rubrics_metrics.description: The characters $, #, %, & (and also \ { }) are special to TeX and must be typed using escape sequences in text: \$ \# \% \& and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain TeX preempts $ # % &; if your manuscript requires these symbols literally type their escaped forms. Backslash and braces are reserved and normally don't appear in copy; they are used for control sequences and grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved characters \ { } must not be used literally
rubrics_metrics.description: The backslash and braces are reserved for control sequences and grouping and should not be used as ordinary characters in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need literal braces or backslashes, use appropriate control sequences or fonts that provide them; in math mode some are available via control sequences. Remember these tokens have syntactic meaning to TeX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct quotation input conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotes and typographic quotes should be input via TeX conventions (e.g., `` for opening quotes and '' for closing quotes) rather than the straight double-quote character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vertical lines and relation signs belong in math mode, double-quote characters should be replaced by `` or ''. Avoid raw " characters in text; use the plain-TeX abbreviations defined in Appendix B (e.g., \lq and \rq) for single quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accents and special letters use TeX accent primitives
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides accent control sequences (\`, \' , \^ , \~ , \= , \. , \u , \v , \H , \t, etc.) and special letters (\oe, \ae, \aa, \o, \l, \ss) to typeset accented and foreign characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accents are implemented using the \accent primitive (e.g., \'#1 ≡ {\accent19 #1}). Accents are positioned relative to the x-height of the current font; if no suitable base character exists the accent appears alone (as if \char{number}). Some accent commands require a space after them unless braced (e.g., use \H{o} to avoid a space). Plain TeX's conventions suit infrequent accents but are not ideal for large-scale multilingual typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Under-accents and special diacritics available
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides under-accents (\c, \d, \b) and other diacritics for languages as part of its accent set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \c{o}, \d{o}, \b{o} for cedilla, dot-under, and bar-under accents respectively. Check Appendix B for exact accent numbers when using \accent directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typewriter font has different behavior and glyphs
rubrics_metrics.description: The \tt (typewriter) font does not form ligatures (ff, fi, fl) and treats dashes and quotes as ordinary ASCII characters; many special accented letters (e.g., \H, \. , \L) may not be available in \tt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because \tt imitates monospaced typewriter output all characters, spaces and symbols have the same width. Use \tt when you want literal ASCII look; if you need certain accents in typewriter style you may have to devise a workaround.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some symbols come from math symbols font and are font-invariant
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols like dagger (\dag), double dagger (\ddag), section (§, \S), and paragraph (¶, \P) are obtained from the math symbols font and look the same in \rm, \sl, \bf, \it, and \tt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These symbols are available uniformly because plain TeX sources them from the math symbol font; consult Appendix B for other non-math symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accent and special-letter conventions belong to the format and fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Accents and special-character conventions are not intrinsic to TeX but belong to the plain TeX format and the Computer Modern fonts; other fonts/formats may use different conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format designers should provide rules for accents and special letters appropriate to their fonts; plain TeX's conventions are fine for infrequent accents but are not recommended for full-scale typesetting of other languages (e.g., ligature-based accent handling might be preferable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension units recognized and their exact definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX understands many units of measure (pt, pc, in, bp, em, cm, mm, dd, cc, sp) with precise conversion factors (e.g., 1 in = 72.27 pt; 65536 sp = 1 pt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct two- or three-letter unit abbreviations. The conversion factors are exact in TeX and internal arithmetic uses sp (scaled point) as the integer unit. See the listed definitions for conversions (pt, pc, in, bp, em, mm, dd, cc, sp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension syntax: {optional sign}{number}{unit} or decimal form
rubrics_metrics.description: To specify a dimension type {optional sign}{number}{unit} or {optional sign}{digit string}.{digit string}{unit}; e.g., 3in, -.013837in, 0.mm, 29pc, +42.1dd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An optional sign may be +, -, or omitted. Spaces before signs/numbers/units are allowed but you must not put spaces inside the digits of a number or between the letters of the unit name. A decimal point can be '.' or ','.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero dimensions must include a unit
rubrics_metrics.description: When a dimension is zero you must still specify a unit (e.g., 0pt or 0in), do not write just '0'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though the unit is irrelevant for zero, TeX's grammar requires a unit name after zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX stores dimensions internally as integer multiples of sp
rubrics_metrics.description: All dimensions are represented internally as integer multiples of the tiny unit sp (scaled point); 65536 sp = 1 pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sp is small relative to visual resolution (wavelength ~100 sp), rounding of a few sp is visually irrelevant. TeX does careful integer arithmetic to ensure identical line/page breaks across implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum legal dimension limit
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX will not handle dimensions whose absolute value is 2^30 sp or more; the maximum legal dimension is slightly less than 16384 pt (about 18.892 feet / 5.7583 meters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid specifying enormous dimensions above TeX's internal limit; typical document layout sizes are far smaller than this cap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'true' units to specify dimensions independent of magnification
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefixing a unit with 'true' (e.g., truept, truein) makes that dimension refer to the final printed size and cancels the current magnification factor for that measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \vskip .5truecm equals \vskip .25cm if \magnification=2000 was in effect. Use true units when you need absolute final sizes regardless of \magnification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnification must be declared before first page and is global
rubrics_metrics.description: Set magnification via \magnification={number} where the number is 1000×the desired factor (e.g., 1200 = 1.2×). This must be given before the first page is shipped to the DVI file; a document can have only one magnification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot apply two different magnifications in the same document. Magnification affects sizes (e.g., \vskip .5cm becomes larger) and the DVI file notes the magnification for the printing routine. Ensure the printing device has the necessary fonts at the requested magnification; large magnifications may require many font shapes and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of fonts constrains magnification
rubrics_metrics.description: You can only use a magnification if the installation/printer has the fonts at the requested magnification; commonly available magsteps are \magstep0, 1, 2, 3 (and maybe 4 or 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check what magnified fonts are available before choosing \magnification. Magnifying may increase resource usage because larger font shapes must be stored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of the \mag primitive and its constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnification is governed by the integer parameter \mag which should be positive and at most 32768; \mag is examined just before the first page shipped, when computing a true dimension, and when closing the DVI file (or shipping pages in non-DVI implementations). \mag must not change after first examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementations may examine \mag at slightly different times, but the key point is that magnification is effectively global and fixed once used; do not change it mid-document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use em for horizontal and ex for vertical font-relative measures
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX recognizes em (the width of a 'quad' in the current font) and ex (the x-height of the current font); em is best for horizontal measurements and ex for vertical measurements that depend on the current font.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: em and ex are font-dependent and vary across fonts even at the same nominal point size. For example in Computer Modern cmr10 em=10pt and ex≈4.3pt; other fonts may differ. Prefer em for horizontal spacing, ex for vertical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keywords/unit names are recognized only in restricted contexts and case-insensitively
rubrics_metrics.description: Unit keywords (pt, in, cm, etc.) and other TeX keywords are recognized only in specific grammatical contexts (e.g., pt after a number in a dimension). Keywords may be given uppercase or mixed case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume tokens like 'pt' are recognized in arbitrary contexts. The manual lists recognized keywords and points to Appendix I for the contexts for each keyword. Unit names are not prefixed by backslashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horizontal and vertical composition via boxes and glue
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX builds pages by composing two-dimensional rectangular boxes (with height, width, depth) and glue, assembling characters into hboxes (horizontal lists) and vboxes (vertical lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single character is a box; use \hbox{...} to lock up a horizontal list and \vbox{...} to build vertical stacks. TeX aligns boxes by reference points/baselines. Use hbox/vbox when you need precise control (e.g., centering, fixed line breaks); otherwise let TeX perform automatic line breaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box dimensions: height, width, depth and possible negative values
rubrics_metrics.description: Each box has height, width, and depth; these numbers can be negative (shadow boxes) and TeX performs arithmetic on them normally (sum widths even if negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fonts may declare negative widths to produce backspaces or special effects; languages with right-to-left reading could be partially handled via negative widths but TeX's line-breaking assumes non-negative word widths. Be cautious when inventing negative dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italic correction must be used when switching from slanted to upright
rubrics_metrics.description: Fonts provide an italic correction value for characters; when moving from a slanted font back to upright you should insert italic correction (via \/) to avoid characters running together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after a slanted word, use \/ before following upright punctuation or letters to add the italic correction. The correction is added to the width of the character if \/ appears immediately after it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black boxes and rule commands (\hrule, \vrule) create filled rectangles
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX can create 'black boxes' (filled rectangles) of arbitrary height/width/depth using \hrule and \vrule, traditionally used for horizontal or vertical rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep black areas modest—printers prefer white space. Even square filled boxes must be called an \hrule or \vrule; rules are discussed further in chapter on boxes and glue.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX's automatic assembly vs manual control
rubrics_metrics.description: For normal text you usually don't need to think about boxes: TeX assembles characters into words, lines, and pages automatically. Use explicit boxes (\hbox, \vbox) only when you want to override TeX's automatic decisions and take full control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using \hbox and \vbox lets you reproduce fine-grained manual typesetting (e.g., centering lines, creating fixed arrangements) but relinquishes automatic line breaking and page building for those regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tokens are instructions; spacing and glue controlled by subsequent tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: Input is processed as a sequence of tokens; e.g., a token 'A' normally means 'put a character box for A at the end of the current hbox', while a token like \vskip means 'skip vertically by the following {dimen}'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that TeX's processing model treats tokens as instructions that consume following tokens (such as dimensions) according to grammar rules. This affects macro design and how you supply arguments (remember tokenization and category codes).
